why: Almost every IT team in France says it works in agile, and BA, data and support offers list Scrum, Kanban and Jira. Interviewers expect you to know the roles and events.
outcome: explain agile values, the Scrum roles, events and artifacts, use a Kanban board, and keep a clean Jira backlog.

lessons.title: Agile in one page
text: Agile means delivering value in small increments, getting feedback early and adapting the plan, instead of specifying everything up front.
Scrum and Kanban are the two most common ways to apply it. Many teams mix them.
points: Agile Manifesto values: individuals and interactions, working software, customer collaboration, responding to change.
Small batches reduce risk: you learn faster when something is wrong.
Done means done: tested, reviewed, deployable.
SAFe scales agile to many teams with program-level planning (PI Planning).

lessons.title: Scrum: roles, events, artifacts
text: Scrum organises work in sprints, usually 2 weeks. The team commits to a sprint goal and delivers a usable increment at the end.
Three accountabilities: the Product Owner maximises value and orders the backlog, the Scrum Master helps the team improve and removes impediments, the Developers build the increment.
points: Sprint Planning: what and how for this sprint, with a sprint goal.
Daily Scrum: 15 minutes to inspect progress toward the goal and adapt.
Sprint Review: show the increment to stakeholders and gather feedback.
Sprint Retrospective: improve how the team works.
Artifacts: Product Backlog, Sprint Backlog, Increment (with the Definition of Done).

lessons.title: Kanban and Jira in practice
text: Kanban visualises work on a board and limits work in progress (WIP) to keep things flowing. It fits support and operations teams with unplanned work.
Jira is the usual tool for both. A clean backlog has small, well-described tickets that anyone can pick up.
points: WIP limits: e.g. at most 3 tickets 'In progress'; finish before starting.
Flow metrics: lead time (request to done), cycle time (start to done), throughput.
Jira hierarchy: Epic > Story / Task / Bug > Sub-task.
Useful JQL: project = ABC AND status = "In Progress" AND assignee = currentUser().

example.code:
JQL examples
project = JOBS AND sprint in openSprints() ORDER BY priority DESC
project = JOBS AND type = Bug AND status != Done AND created >= -14d
assignee = currentUser() AND resolution = Unresolved

pitfalls: Daily Scrum turning into a status report for a manager.
Sprints with no goal, just a list of tickets.
Tickets too big to finish in a sprint.

exercises.q: Your support team gets urgent tickets every day. Scrum or Kanban? Why?
exercises.answer: Kanban: work arrives continuously and unpredictably, so fixed sprints would be broken constantly. A board with WIP limits and service classes (urgent, standard) fits better.

exercises.q: Write a JQL query for unresolved bugs created in the last 7 days in project JOBS, highest priority first.
exercises.answer: project = JOBS AND type = Bug AND resolution = Unresolved AND created >= -7d ORDER BY priority DESC

exercises.q: In a retrospective the team says 'tickets are always unclear'. Propose an action.
exercises.answer: Agree on a Definition of Ready (user story format, acceptance criteria, mock-up if UI) and hold a short weekly backlog refinement with the PO before planning.

interview.q: What does the Product Owner do?
interview.a: Owns the product backlog and its order, represents users and stakeholders, defines what is valuable, writes or clarifies stories with acceptance criteria and accepts the delivered work.

interview.q: What is the Definition of Done?
interview.a: A shared checklist that every increment must meet to be considered done, for example code reviewed, tests passing, documentation updated, deployed to staging.

Scrum uses fixed sprints, defined roles and events and commits to a sprint goal. Kanban has continuous flow, no prescribed roles, and limits work in progress. Scrum suits planned product work; Kanban suits continuous, unpredictable work such as support.
